title: This Beautifully Weird Necklace Is Secretly a USB Drive
gist: Noware, a two-person New York hardware outfit run by Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain, ships its Puff USB-drive necklace in October after a 2025 prototype post drew over a million views and thousands of waitlist signups. The device costs $179 for 128 GB against roughly $30 for a comparable basic flash drive, a premium the founders attribute partly to memory prices inflated by the AI boom.

themes.theme: Memory pricing squeezed by AI demand

insights.claim: Noware's Puff USB necklace sells for $179 with only 128 GB of storage against roughly $30 for a basic flash drive of similar capacity, and the founders attribute part of that premium to the inflated cost of memory driven by the AI boom.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Independent confirmation from small hardware makers that AI datacenter demand is raising component costs at the consumer end — a margin headwind for every low-volume device startup and a tailwind for memory suppliers.
insights.quote: They blame it partially on the inflated cost of memory right now, thanks to the AI boom.
insights.locator: The necklace’s biggest drawback is its price

insights.claim: Noware's founders expect the Puff's price to fall over time and say future iterations may include cheaper variants such as a nonmetal version, framing the current $179 tag as an existence-proof price rather than a target price.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Cost-down depends on memory prices easing and volume scaling — watch whether small-batch consumer hardware can reprice if NAND stays tight.
insights.quote: We want it to get cheaper over time, but we're just trying to make it exist first
insights.locator: The duo doesn’t want the Puff to remain that expensive

insights.claim: Noware's early Puff prototype post in 2025 racked up over a million views and thousands of waitlist signups, and the team then spent roughly a year converting that attention into mass production with shipping set for October.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: A roughly 12-month gap between viral demand signal and first shipment is the realistic conversion lag for social-first hardware — relevant when underwriting waitlist-driven consumer hardware.
insights.locator: When Harry Isaac and Sebastian Bidegain

insights.claim: Neither Noware founder has previously had a wide product release, with prior work limited to viral one-offs like a bubble-shooting electric scooter, a vape camera and a lo-fi sampler built into a rock — meaning the October launch is an unproven manufacturing execution.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: First-time-at-scale manufacturing is where most viral hardware fails; treat the October ship date as the real risk milestone.
insights.locator: Neither has had a wide release for their products before

insights.claim: The Puff has no internal battery, which the reviewer argues lets the USB drive persist as jewelry far longer than the usable life of most consumer electronics.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Battery-free design sidesteps the degradation clock that kills resale and longevity in wearables — a differentiator worth watching as durability becomes a purchase criterion.
insights.quote: The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery, so the USB drive can live as a piece of jewelry far longer than the expiration date of most electronics.
insights.locator: The Puff doesn’t have an internal battery

insights.claim: The Puff includes a small center screen that displays customizable animations when plugged into a phone or laptop, with custom software anyone can use to craft their own designs, adding a user-generated content layer to a storage accessory.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: Turning a commodity flash drive into a customizable display object is the mechanism for the price premium — a template for differentiating commoditized hardware.
insights.locator: The small screen in the middle of the necklace

insights.claim: Noware positions the Puff both as pure fashion — marketing shows it clipped to a purse where a Labubu might have sat last year — and as a working tool for photographers, DJs and IT people who still use flash drives in their workflow.
insights.speaker: Reece Rogers
insights.so_what: The dual fashion-accessory and pro-tool positioning is a bet that collectible-object demand (the Labubu trade) can be captured by functional electronics.
insights.quote: On one end, I want anyone to be able to wear it, just if they think it's pretty
insights.locator: Noware’s marketing materials show a cool girl
